entities.name: Lotus Sutra (Saddharmapundarika Sutra)
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
One of the most influential and widely venerated Mahayana Buddhist sutras, composed c. 100 CE and translated into Chinese by Kumarajiva in 406 CE. The Lotus Sutra teaches that all Buddhist paths (shravaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva) are ultimately one vehicle (ekayana) leading to Buddhahood; that the Buddha's lifespan is immeasurably long (he merely appears to die as a "skillful means" to motivate beings); and that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and can attain complete enlightenment.

These revolutionary ideas became the foundation of multiple East Asian Buddhist schools: Tiantai/Tendai (which considers the Lotus Sutra the supreme teaching), Nichiren Buddhism (which chants its title as a devotional practice), and influenced Zen and Pure Land thought. The sutra's literary brilliance — cosmic visions, parables, dramatic narratives — matches its philosophical depth.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Lotus Sutra's teachings on the ultimate unity of Buddhist paths and the inherent Buddha-nature of all sentient beings influenced the development of multiple East Asian Buddhist schools, including Tiantai/Tendai and Nichiren Buddhism. Its devotional practice has been chanted by millions for centuries.
